Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 110, verse 1:

(p-137)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat an-Nasr (The Divine Support)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the help of Allah comes, and the conquest﴾.

In it is the mention of nasr (help, victory) and fath (conquest, opening), although each of them is linked to the other: with every nasr there is a fath, and with every fath there is a nasr.

So are they mutually necessary, or not?

Just as nasr comes attributed to Allah, the Exalted, fath comes unrestricted.

First: the scholars agree that this surah was revealed after the conquest of Makkah.

It is known that the conquest of Makkah was preceded by several conquests (futuh).

Among them is the conquest of Khaybar, and among them is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, which Allah, the Exalted, named a fath in His saying: ﴿So He knew what you did not know, and He made, besides that, a near conquest﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

Nasr occurs in the battlefield, occurs through proof and authority, and occurs through the repelling of the enemy, as in the case of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good. And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting, and Allah is ever Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25].

And as in the case of the Jews, His saying: ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts. A party you killed, and you took captive a party﴾, ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, and their wealth, and a land you had not trodden. And ever is Allah, over all things, Competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26-27].

So nasr is a truth from Allah: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [Ali Imran: 126].

The Muslims knew this, as His saying: ﴿They were touched by hardship and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], so they were longing for the nasr.

(p-138)

And the answer comes to them: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214].

And there came his saying (ﷺ): "I have been supported with terror, a distance of a month's journey."

And He, the Exalted, said to Musa and his brother: ﴿Fear not; indeed I am with you both, Hearing and Seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. So this is nasr of companionship and support, and nasr here is general.

Likewise, fath in religion is through the spread of Islam, and the greatest of conquests are two: the conquest of al-Hudaybiyah and the conquest of Makkah.

For the first is a preparation for the second, and the second is the ending of the state of shirk in the Peninsula, and this indicates the intended generality in nasr and fath.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 110, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾. It seems that people came from every direction, even from Yemen, and this indicates the completeness of the da'wah (call to Islam) and the success of the message.

What supports this is the revelation of the verse: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favor upon you, and have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and its descent was during the Hajj of that year.

It is also noted that victory is mentioned here in the form "the victory of Allah" (naṣr Allāh), whereas elsewhere it is mentioned as "victory" (naṣr) alone: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 10].

It is well known that this idafah (annexation, construction of the genitive) here carries the sense of completion and perfection, as in "the House of Allah" (bayt Allah). Although all mosques are houses of Allah, this indicates the whole of victory, or the complete totality of victory, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for al-fath (the conquest), it has been said here that it is the conquest of Makkah, and it has been said that it is the conquest of cities and others.

Numerous conquests before Makkah have already been alluded to.

There are conquests promised after the conquest of Makkah, which the Prophet (ﷺ) specified, among them in the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when they were digging the trench (al-Khandaq) and a hard rock obstructed them and overwhelmed them, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to it. He took water, rinsed his mouth, supplicated as much as Allah willed him to supplicate, then struck, and it became like a heap of sand.

Ibn Kathir narrated it through several different reports and chains, and all of them mention that he (ﷺ) struck three blows, and a flash of light appeared under each blow, and he (ﷺ) said "Allahu akbar" at each one. They asked him, and he said: "At the first: 'I have been given the keys of Persia,'" and he mentioned Yemen and al-Sham. All these reports are not free from discussion, but because of their multiplicity, some strengthen others.

The strongest of them is the report of al-Nasa'i with his chain, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the digging of the trench, a rock appeared to them that came between them and the digging. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood, took the pickaxe, placed his cloak at the side of the trench, and said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice; none can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-An'am: 115]. A third of the stone broke off, while Salman al-Farisi was standing watching. A flash of light appeared with the blow of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he struck a second time and recited what he had recited first, and a flash appeared again. Then the third time, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out, the stone having been shattered. He took his cloak and sat down. Salman asked him, when he saw the three flashes: He said to him: 'Did you see that?' He said: 'Yes, by Him who sent you with the truth, O Messenger of Allah.' So he informed them that in the first, the cities of Kisra (Chosroes) and what surrounds them, and many cities, were raised for him until he saw them with his own eyes. They said: 'Pray to Allah for us that He open them to us.' So he prayed for them. In the second, the cities of Caesar (Qayṣar) and what surrounds them were raised for him, and in the third, the cities of Abyssinia (al-Habashah). All of them asked him (ﷺ) to pray for them that they be opened to them, and he prayed for them except for Abyssinia, and he (ﷺ) said: 'Leave Abyssinia while it leaves you, and leave the Turks while they leave you.'" End of the summary.

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Kathir both narrated it at greater length. These reports, although they may be open to critique, yet in the Muwatta' there is what admits no critique, and there is no doubt about its authenticity or its indication. It is what Malik narrated from Hisham from 'Urwah from his father from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr from Sufyan ibn Abi Zuhayr, that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Yemen will be conquered, and a people will come who will ride (their camels) away, taking their families and whoever obeys them, and Madinah is better for them, if they only knew. And al-Sham will be conquered, and a people will come who will ride away, taking their families and whoever obeys them, and Madinah is better for them, if they only knew. And Iraq will be conquered, and a people will come who will ride away, taking their families and whoever obeys them, and Madinah is better for them, if they only knew.'"

This is a sound and explicit text from him (ﷺ), during his lifetime, about the conquest of Yemen, al-Sham, and Iraq, and all of them were conquered only after him (ﷺ), except Yemen.

This view is supported by what Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madinah, he said: 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, the victory of Allah and the conquest has come, the people of Yemen have come.'" It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are the people of Yemen?" He said: "A people whose hearts are tender and whose natures are gentle; faith is Yamani, understanding is Yamani, and wisdom is Yamani." Ibn Kathir narrated it from him.

The conquest of Makkah took place in the eighth year after the Hijrah, and the delegations came in the multitudes into the religion of Allah in the ninth year. The delegation of Yemen came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) sent his governors to Yemen after the conquest of Makkah, and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) came to him from Yemen in the tenth year during the season of Hajj. Thus Yemen was conquered after the conquest of Makkah during his lifetime (ﷺ).

Accordingly, there were conquests that occurred after the conquest of Makkah, which the words ﴿and the conquest﴾ may include here, and it is not restricted to the conquest of Makkah as some have said.

It may also be taken by way of indication (dalalat al-ima'): the promise of extensive conquests over vast regions, from His saying: ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]; because coming from every deep pass indicates coming to the Hajj from afar, and coming to the Hajj indicates Islam, and thus indicates the arrival of Muslims from far away. This is the point of inference, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 110, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.﴾ The discussion of *tasbih* (glorification), its object, and its morphology has already been presented.

Here He combined the *tasbih* with the praise of Allah, and in this there is a subtle connection to the beginning of the surah and its theme. The surah indicates the completion of the mission of the Message through the coming of the help of Allah to His Prophet ﷺ, to the believers, and to His religion, and through the coming of the general conquest over the lands of Allah, either in actuality or as a true promise, as has already been mentioned. This is a blessing that requires thanks, and its Giver deserves praise.

Thus the glorification was joined with praise in return for that. And His saying ﴿with the praise of your Lord﴾ indicates that He, glory be to Him, is the Giver of blessings, as He said in Surah ad-Duha: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested [you].﴾ [Ad-Duha: 3]

(p. 141) And His saying in Surah Iqra': ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [Al-Alaq: 1], and its repetition: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ [Al-Alaq: 3]; because the attribute of lordship (*rububiyyah*) indicates bestowal of favours.

As for His saying ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾, some have said: seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*) is for a sin, so what is the sin? The discussion of the infallibility (*ismah*) of the prophets, peace be upon them, has already been presented at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ [Ash-Sharh: 2].

Among what deserves mention is that repentance (*tawbah*) is the call of the messengers. If we begin with Adam, peace be upon him, with his story, in it is: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 37], and the cause of that repentance is known.

Then Nuh, peace be upon him, says: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my home as a believer and the believing men and believing women﴾ [Nuh: 28], to the end of the verse.

And Ibrahim, peace be upon him, says: ﴿And show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 128].

On this basis some scholars said: seeking forgiveness is itself an act of worship, like glorification, so its occurrence does not necessarily imply the existence of a sin.

It was also said: it is a teaching for his community.

It was said: it is a raising of his ranks ﷺ.

It has come in the Sunnah that he ﷺ said: "Repent to Allah, for I repent to Allah a hundred times a day." So this may also fall under the category of increasing in good and turning back to Allah.

A note:

It has come in the exegesis (*tafsir*, explanation of the Qur'an) according to all that since this surah was revealed, he ﷺ did not leave off saying: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You." 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He was interpreting the Qur'an" (*yatawwalu al-Qur'an*), i.e., explaining it and acting upon it.

Abu Hayyan transmitted from az-Zamakhshari that he said: The command to seek forgiveness along with glorification is a completion of the command (p. 142) with what is the foundation of the matter of the religion, from combining obedience with guarding against disobedience. And so that his being commanded with that, together with his infallibility, would be a kindness (*lutf*) to his community. And because seeking forgiveness is part of humility and the subduing of the self, it is an act of worship in itself.

In this there is a call to attention for the people of *adhkar* (remembrances) and *awrad* (litanies) who are eager for the constancy of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, since this was among the things he ﷺ most constantly persisted in. This is in addition to what was reported from him ﷺ regarding the remembrances of the morning and evening, without being constant upon the mention of a single name of the names of Allah, the Exalted, alone, in isolation from what no sound or explicit text has been reported for.

There is no doubt that all good lies in following (*ittiba'*), not in innovation (*ibtida'*). And what greater good is there than what Allah chose for His Prophet ﷺ at the end of his life, commanding him with it, while he himself constantly adhered to it?

We said "at the end of his life" because he ﷺ died a short time after it.

In this verse there is the indication of allusion (*dalalat al-iima'*), as they said, and the implicative indication (*dalalat al-iltizam*), as was reported from Ibn 'Abbas in the story of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, with the senior Emigrants and Helpers, when he would permit him to sit with them and would look at their faces. They asked him and said: "We have children his age." He said: "It is from where you know."

On a day when they gathered before him, 'Umar summoned him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I knew that he had only summoned me for a matter." So he asked them about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the help of Allah has come and the conquest﴾, the surah to its end.

They said: "It is glad tidings of the conquest and the help." He said: "What do you say, O Ibn 'Abbas?"

He said: I said, "No, by Allah, it informs us of the approaching death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while he is among us."

'Umar said: "I do not know anything in it except what you have said," i.e., that he ﷺ came for a mission, and it has been completed by the coming of the help and the conquest and the entry into the religion in multitudes.

On this basis, he has fulfilled the trust and conveyed the Message. So he should prepare to meet his Lord, to receive the reward of his deed. This is a derivation of the utmost subtlety, and an explanation of the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Or an understanding that Allah gives to whomever He wills in the Book of Allah."
